title: The Efficacy and Safety of Dalfampridine on Cognition and Fatigue in People With Multiple Sclerosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authors: Halabi MH, Alromayan R, Almutairi M, Alasmari H, AlGhamdi MA, Makkawi S
abstract: BACKGROUND: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disease affecting the central nervous system. People with MS frequently experience cognitive dysfunction and fatigue. Dalfampridine (DAL), a potassium channel blocker, is US Food and Drug Administration-approved for the treatment of walking impairment in people with MS. It may also enhance nerve conduction in regions associated with fatigue and cognitive dysfunction. This study aims to evaluate DAL's efficacy in improving these symptoms, as well as its safety profile, in people with MS. METHODS: A systematic search was conducted across MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, Scopus, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Web of Science, covering all records from database inception through April 1, 2024. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing DAL with placebo in people with MS and reporting impaired cognition and fatigue were included. A random-effects model was used to calculate the risk ratio (RR), standardized mean difference (SMD), and mean difference (MD) with 95% CIs. RESULTS: Of 1329 studies identified, 13 RCTs involving a total of 827 people with MS were included. DAL demonstrated a significant improvement in cognitive symptoms (SMD = 0.21; 95% CI, 0.04-0.38; P = .01; I² = 6%). However, no significant difference was observed between DAL and placebo in reducing fatigue (MD = 3.70; 95% CI, -4.37 to 11.77;P = .37; I² = 19%). Safety measures were comparable, with no significant difference in adverse events (RR = 1.11; 95% CI, 0.99-1.25; P = .08; I² = 0%). CONCLUSIONS: People with MS receiving DAL demonstrated significant improvement in cognitive symptoms; however, further studies are warranted to validate and confirm this finding.

title: Underwater Endoscopic Mucosal Resection for Serrated Lesions: A Systematic Review and Single-Arm Meta-Analysis.
authors: Almeida R, Santo P, Souza M, Nobre R, Safatle-Ribeiro AV, Maluf-Filho F, Lenz L
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Sessile serrated lesions (SSLs) are established colorectal cancer precursors, and complete removal is essential. Although underwater endoscopic mucosal resection (UEMR) has gained acceptance for nonpedunculated colorectal lesions, evidence specific to SSLs remains limited. We conducted a systematic review and single-arm meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy and safety of UEMR for SSLs. METHODS: PubMed, EMBASE, and Cochrane databases were searched through June 2025 for studies reporting UEMR outcomes in SSLs. The primary outcome was R0 resection. Secondary outcomes included en bloc resection, complete resection, recurrence, and adverse events (AEs). Pooled proportions with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was assessed with I2. RESULTS: Seven observational studies including 581 lesions were analyzed. Median lesion size ranged from 12 to 24.6 mm. R0 resection was achieved in 72.5% (95% CI, 58.4-83.2), decreasing to 63.6% for lesions ≥10 mm. The pooled complete resection rate was 90.5% (95% CI, 69.6-100) en bloc resection rate was 80.4% (95% CI, 65.0-90.1). AEs were uncommon, with a pooled incidence of 0.56% (95% CI, 0-1.74), including six delayed bleeding events and five perforations. Recurrence was assessed in three studies (with a pooled rate of 2.37% (95% CI, 1.24-4.49; I2 = 0%). CONCLUSIONS: UEMR is a safe and effective technique for resection of SSLs, demonstrating high complete resection rates, acceptable en bloc and R0 rates, and low recurrence and AE incidence. Randomized comparative studies are warranted to better define its role among resection strategies. Trial Registration: PROSPERO: CRD420252083459.

title: Modern cell-based assays for biomedical research: from conventional methods to AI-driven high content analysis.
authors: Venkataramaiah C
abstract: In vitro cell-based assays are fundamental tools in biomedical research, supporting investigations of cellular physiology, disease mechanisms, drug discovery, toxicology, regenerative medicine, and precision therapeutics. However, conventional two-dimensional (2D) cell culture models often fail to recapitulate the structural complexity and physiological functions of native tissues, prompting the development of advanced platforms, including three-dimensional (3D) cultures, organoids, organ-on-a-chip technologies, and microphysiological systems. Recent advances in cell viability and cytotoxicity assessment, functional cellular analysis, molecular profiling, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based functional genomics, high-content imaging, flow cytometry, single-cell and spatial multi-omics, and automated high-throughput screening have expanded the analytical capabilities of cell-based assays. Furthermore, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted image analysis and computational biology has enhanced cellular phenotyping, biomarker discovery, and mechanistic investigation, with the potential to improve the prediction of therapeutic efficacy and toxicity. Nevertheless, challenges related to physiological relevance, technical variability, inadequate standardization, high operational costs, scalability, poor reproducibility, cell-line misidentification, batch-to-batch variation, and inconsistent reporting continue to hinder translational applications. Future progress will depend on integrating physiologically relevant models with AI-driven analytics, spatial multi-omics, digital pathology, automated screening, and microphysiological systems. Standardized protocols, harmonized reporting practices, and interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential to improve reproducibility, strengthen regulatory acceptance, advance precision medicine, and reduce reliance on animal experimentation. In this context, this review critically evaluates conventional and emerging in vitro cell-based assays, emphasizing their biological principles, analytical capabilities, translational applications, and practical limitations, while highlighting future opportunities to improve predictive accuracy, reproducibility, and clinical translation.

title: Natural polysaccharides targeting gut microbiota in renal fibrosis: Novel molecular mechanisms and therapeutic strategies.
authors: Yu QQ, Li X, Fang HB, Zhang YL, Yang J, Miao H, Liu LM, Zhao YY
abstract: Kidney disease, including acute kidney injury (AKI) and chronic kidney disease (CKD), represent a major global health burden and are associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. AKI is an overwhelming complication of acute disease that leads to the CKD development and ultimately progresses to end-stage renal disease. AKI and CKD are inter-related clinical and pathophysiological disorders. Current treatments, including dialysis and transplantation, are costly and not curative. Natural polysaccharides, widely distributed in medicinal plants and fungi, are important active components with broad healthcare applications. As a natural modulator of gut microbiota (GM), natural polysaccharides play an important role in regulating intestinal inflammation and gut microbial dysbiosis. This review summarizes the pathogenesis and underlying molecular mechanisms of renal fibrosis associated with GM dysbiosis, providing therapeutic strategies and targets for polysaccharide remodeling of the GM to improve kidney disease. We further systematically present the beneficial effects of natural polysaccharides on kidney disease through various molecular mechanisms, such as Toll-like receptor 4, G-protein-coupled receptors, NOD-, LRR- and pyrin domain-containing protein 3 inflammasome, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor, IƙB/NF-ƙB and Keap1/Nrf2 signaling pathways via regulating gut microbial-derived metabolites, such as lipopolysaccharide, short-chain fatty acids, and uremic toxins. These studies expand the understanding of the therapeutic effects and underlying molecular mechanism of natural polysaccharides on kidney disease and expound a clear pathophysiological rationale for the treatment of kidney disease. This review provides targeted therapeutic strategies for kidney disease prevention and management by modulating GM, highlighting the potential of natural polysaccharides as prebiotics in clinical practice.

title: Kidney effects of inhaled nitric oxide in critically ill patients: from pathophysiological considerations to clinical implications.
authors: Robert A, Gonze A, Bulpa P, Hauquiert B
abstract: Inhaled nitric oxide is widely used as a selective pulmonary vasodilator in critical care, yet its renal effects remain controversial. While existing reviews mostly focus on indications for inhaled nitric oxide and its impact on outcomes, limited data exist on its renal effects, since it was thought to act only locally in the lungs. This review examine the clinical evidence regarding kidney outcomes associated with inhaled nitric oxide across major indications and provide an integrated mechanistic analysis of nitric oxide signaling in renal physiology and pathophysiology. Nitric oxide is produced by nitric oxide synthases using L-arginine as a substrate. It acts as a smooth muscle relaxation factor and ultimately causes vasodilation through its effect on cyclic guanosine monophosphate. Nitric oxide plays a pivotal role in renal hemodynamic regulation, glomerular filtration, tubular function, and microcirculatory homeostasis. The net renal effect of inhaled nitric oxide likely reflects the balance between improved nitric oxide signaling and oxidative stress generation. Available clinical data suggest that the renal impact of inhaled nitric oxide is context-dependent. In acute respiratory distress syndrome, higher-level evidence indicates a potential increase in acute kidney injury, possibly related to oxidative and nitrosative stress. Conversely, in cardiac bypass surgery, inhaled nitric oxide may confer nephroprotection by restoring nitric oxide bioavailability during hemolysis and free hemoglobin-mediated nitric oxide scavenging. In other conditions, including organ transplantation, pulmonary hypertension, sepsis, and hemolytic disorders, evidence remains limited or inconclusive. Overall, current evidence does not support a uniform renal effect of inhaled nitric oxide, indicating the need for prospective studies with predefined renal endpoints to clarify its clinical relevance.

title: Environmental microbial exposure as an under-measured exposome domain: Links to host microbiomes, immune regulation, and disease epidemiology.
authors: Parekh Y, Parmar V
journal: Journal of environmental health science & engineering
abstract: Environmental microbial exposure is an under-measured biological component of the exposome and a plausible determinant of immune-mediated disease patterns. Humans encounter microbial communities and products from soil, air, water, vegetation, animals, food systems, farms, indoor dust, healthcare settings, schools, and urban built environments. These exposures may influence gut, skin, airway, oral, and mucosal microbiomes and thereby alter epithelial barrier function, immune tolerance, inflammatory thresholds, and microbial metabolite production. This structured mechanistic narrative review integrates direct environmental-exposure studies, environment-to-host microbiome studies, host-microbiome mechanistic evidence, and translational frameworks. The clearest convergence occurs in asthma and allergic disease, where early-life farm exposure, endotoxin-rich dust, environmental microbial diversity, innate immune modulation, and epithelial A20 regulation support a coherent exposure-response model. Evidence for inflammatory bowel disease and broader respiratory outcomes is biologically credible but less direct, whereas metabolic and systemic inflammatory outcomes remain largely supported by host-microbiome and metabolite mechanisms rather than direct environmental exposure studies. The review therefore distinguishes evidence maturity and mechanistic proximity rather than treating all disease categories equally. It further positions pollution, urbanization, building design, biodiversity loss, diet, antibiotics, and socioeconomic conditions as active modifiers of microbial exposure and host response. Future studies should integrate direct environmental sampling with body-site microbiome profiling, functional multi-omics, immune and barrier biomarkers, geospatial exposure assessment, source tracking, repeated measures, and explicit causal-inference designs. Environmental microbial exposure should be treated neither as uniformly beneficial nor harmful, but as a measurable, context-dependent exposome domain whose health effects depend on composition, dose, timing, route, co-exposures, and host susceptibility.

title: Breast cancer cell motility speed measurement using in vitro assays: a systematic scoping review of current knowledge.
authors: Maran MM, Shelling AN, Wu Z, Laking G
abstract: PURPOSE: This systematic scoping review evaluates contemporary advancements in the design and clinical application of lab-on-a-chip (LOC) microdevices specialised for measuring breast cancer cell motility parameters. It tracks the engineering frontiers of biomimetic systems and addresses their predictive potential in oncology research. METHODS: Utilising the PRISMA scoping review framework, a systematic database screening was executed to capture primary research articles published over a twelve-year retrospective window from 2016 to 2026. Sourced literature was subjected to thematic synthesis. The inclusion criteria targeted seven baseline parameters: (1) LOC architectures as functional in vitro assays, (2) dynamic cell migration tracking, (3) structural tumour microenvironment mimics, (4) real-time single-cell velocity quantification, (5) gravity-driven fluidic perfusion setups, (6) cellular plasticity profiling, and (7) oestrogen-linked hormone receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer models. RESULTS: The systematic search identified in vitro configurations modelling tumour growth boundaries, localised angiogenesis, lymphatic vessel transport, transendothelial intravasation/extravasation, and organ-specific metastasis niches. Recent design advances emphasise three-dimensional (3D) matrix-based microfluidic platforms that replicate matrix stiffness and interfacial friction parameters to capture cell behaviours under fluid shear stress.The literature re-screening revealed that no published studies met all seven analytical criteria required to integrate real-time, single-cell-speed calculations within a unidirectional, gravity-driven dynamic flow loop tailored exclusively for ER+ breast cancer subtyping. CONCLUSION: This review uncovers a technological and biological knowledge gap regarding integrated, low-cost microfluidic assays that can automate individual cell trajectory tracking under physiological flow conditions. Resolving this constraint by bridging advanced single-cell engineering chips with transcriptomic phenotyping and interactive clinical dashboards represents a milestone to validate cell motility as an independent prognostic biomarker, to enable personalised, precision treatment strategies.

title: Engineering copper homeostasis for microenvironment-adaptive therapy in inflammation-driven disorders.
authors: Ding F, Liu J, Liu M, Huang H, Tang H, Zhong J, Liu C, Liu Z
abstract: Inflammation-driven disorders (IDDs) arise from distinct initiating events, yet many persist because immune activation, oxidative and metabolic stress, regulated cell death, and tissue remodeling form self-reinforcing local niches. Copper connects these processes through its roles as a cuproenzyme cofactor, redox-active species and dynamically trafficked regulatory metal. Its therapeutic significance, however, is determined by disease stage, cell type, subcellular distribution and chemical state. Copper deficiency, excess or mislocalization may therefore be adaptive, protective or pathogenic in different contexts. This review develops a disease- and copper-state-specific framework that links copper homeostasis to therapeutic platform design. We first examine inflammation-associated remodeling of copper trafficking and compare representative copper states in autoimmune joint disease, metabolic inflammation, fibrosis, inflammation-associated cancer and infection-associated tissue repair. We then critically evaluate copper-dependent and copper-sensitive mechanisms governing inflammatory mediator availability, immune-cell programming and checkpoint regulation, regulated cell death, angiogenesis and stromal remodeling, while distinguishing direct mechanistic evidence from model-dependent inference. Building on this analysis, we compare pharmacological modulators with nanocarriers, copper-containing active materials and local copper-sequestering platforms that implement copper chelation or sequestration, controlled copper delivery or release, intracellular redistribution, and catalytic activation or nanozyme-like redox regulation. We further outline how pathological copper pools, activation cues, release kinetics, speciation, biodistribution and target engagement should be measured so that precision is demonstrated rather than inferred from material composition. This framework positions copper modulation as a context-specific complement to existing therapy and defines the mechanistic, analytical and translational evidence required for microenvironment-adaptive treatment of IDDs.

title: A let-7a-5p-engineered extracellular vesicle-laden bioactive scaffold promotes immunomodulation and regeneration of segmental tracheal defects.
authors: Liu B, Wei N, Liang L, Shi Z, Liu P, Zeng T, Zhang H, Zhang H
abstract: Segmental tracheal defects resulting from trauma, tumor resection, or congenital malformations pose significant challenges for reconstruction. Persistent post-injury inflammation, inadequate neovascularization, and delayed epithelial restoration contribute to the formation of granulation tissue and subsequent graft failure. In this study, we developed a bioactive tracheal scaffold for sustained local delivery of let-7a-5p-engineered extracellular vesicles (let-7a-5p-EVs) to modulate the regenerative microenvironment during tracheal repair. The scaffold was constructed by integrating a mechanically optimized polycaprolactone (PCL) framework with a 20% Pluronic F127 hydrogel, which served as a local reservoir for EV retention and sustained release. Let-7a-5p-EVs were generated from lentivirally engineered human gingiva-derived mesenchymal stem cells and showed typical EV morphology, representative EV marker expression, and efficient uptake by airway epithelial cells. In vitro, let-7a-5p-EVs enhanced airway epithelial cell migration and shifted lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced macrophages from a pro-inflammatory M1-like phenotype toward a reparative M2-like phenotype, accompanied by reduced inflammatory cytokine expression. In a rabbit segmental tracheal defect model, the let-7a-5p-EV-laden scaffold enhanced neovascularization, mitigated local inflammatory responses, promoted mucociliary epithelial reconstruction, and maintained airway patency. The let-7a-5p-EV scaffold improved biomechanical recovery, and increased survival rates. Transcriptomic profiling and molecular validation indicated that these effects were associated with the attenuation of nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB)-associated inflammatory activation, as evidenced by reduced p65 phosphorylation and nuclear localization. These findings demonstrate that sustained local delivery of engineered EVs from a mechanically competent bioactive scaffold provides an effective immunomodulatory strategy for the regenerative repair of segmental tracheal defects and offers translational potential for functional airway reconstruction.

title: Association of retinal abnormalities and adverse cardiac events in patients with coronary artery disease and type 2 diabetes.
authors: Qian HMK, Konttinen AKE, Holmström LTA, Wirkkala JPK, King ISE, Lepojärvi ES, Tulppo MP, Perkiömäki JS
abstract: BACKGROUND: The aim of this study was to evaluate the association of retinal abnormalities and cardiac mortality in patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) and type 2 diabetes (DM). METHODS: The ARTEMIS study is a prospective cohort study of 1,946 patients (68% male; mean age 66.9 ± 8.6 years) diagnosed with CAD. Type 2 DM was diagnosed in 834 patients (43%), and 525 (27%) of them had retinal images available. RESULTS: During mean follow-up of 8.7 ± 2.2 years, 54 cardiac deaths occurred. From all analyzed retinal abnormalities, diabetic retinopathy (DR) was associated with cardiac death (p = 0.005). DR was independently associated with increased risk of cardiac death (DR 16.2% vs. non-DR 8.4%; hazard ratio [HR] 2.0, 95% CI: 1.0-4.0, p = 0.04) when adjusted with confounding factors. DR was associated with sudden cardiac death (SCD) (DR 8.5% vs. non-DR 3.8%; HR 2.9, 95% CI: 1.1-7.7, p = 0.03) but not with non-sudden cardiac death (DR 7.7% vs. non-DR 4.6%; HR 1.5, 95% CI: 0.6-3.9, p = 0.5). Interestingly, increased hs-TnT, measured in stable phase of CAD, was also associated with DR (p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: DR seems to be associated with cardiac death, and more specifically, with SCD in patients with CAD and type 2 DM. DR might be a novel marker of microvascular cardiac disease resulting in ongoing myocardial injury and SCD.

title: A ratiometric dual-modal photoacoustic and near-infrared fluorescence probe for in vivo spatiotemporal mapping of butyrylcholinesterase in Alzheimer's disease.
authors: Meng Y, Wang C, Hu Y, Zhou H, Zhou J, Gao W, Xing W, Shu X
abstract: Butyrylcholinesterase (BChE) is a critical biomarker for the progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology; however, real-time visualization of its dynamic activity changes in deep biological tissues remains highly challenging. Herein, we report the development of BChE-PA, a novel hemicyanine-based dual-modal probe for the ratiometric detection of BChE through integrated near-infrared (NIR) fluorescence and photoacoustic (PA) imaging. The probe design utilizes a specific cyclopropanecarbonyl recognition moiety that effectively masks the internal charge transfer (ICT) process of the fluorophore. Enzymatic cleavage of the cyclopropanecarbonyl group by BChE restores the ICT effect and extends the molecular π-conjugation, triggering a significant 93 nm bathochromic shift in absorption (from 622 nm to 715 nm) and a dramatic NIR fluorescence "turn-on" response. BChE-PA exhibits an exceptional detection limit of 0.03 U/mL and high selectivity over competing esterases. By leveraging the ratiometric PA signal (PA755/PA680), we successfully performed self-calibrating, deep-tissue mapping of elevated BChE levels in the brains of APP/PS1 transgenic mice. This dual-modal platform provides a robust tool for the spatiotemporal tracking of BChE, bridging the gap between molecular environmental surveillance and clinical neuroimaging.

title: Baicalin alleviates renal interstitial fibrosis by targeting SIRT1/HIF-1α signaling pathway.
authors: Zhao S, Zhang Q, Li X, Wang M, Xu A, Zhang J
abstract: UNLABELLED: RENAL INTERSTITIAL FIBROSIS IS A DEFINING FEATURE OF PROGRESSIVE CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE: (CKD) with no effective therapeutic drugs in the clinic. Baicalin (BA) is a natural product sourced from Scutellaria baicalensis and has been proven to treat renal fibrosis and multiple kidney diseases. However, the anti-renal fibrosis effects of BA have not been systematically studied, and its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. AIM OF STUDY: This study aims to investigate the role of BA in renal interstitial fibrosis and its potential pharmacological mechanism. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The model of unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) mouse and TGF-β-induced cells were employed to evaluate the anti-fibrotic effect of baicalin in vivo and in vitro, respectively. The molecular docking, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), and cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) were used to verify the relationship of BA and its specific target, Sirtuin 1 (SIRT1). The gene-knockdown cells, RNA-sequence analysis, western blotting assay, and RT-qPCR analysis were performed to clarify the BA-SIRT1 interaction and explore its underlying pharmacological mechanisms. RESULTS: BA significantly ameliorated renal fibrosis and promoted renal function in UUO mice, with suppressing fibroblast activation in cultured cells. The results of molecular docking, SPR, and CETSA suggested that SIRT1 is a specific target of BA. The anti-fibrotic effects of BA were abolished after SIRT1 was knocked down. The following RNA sequencing and western blotting analysis revealed that BA inhibits the TGF-β1-induced HIF-α signaling pathway via targeting SIRT1. CONCLUSIONS: This study indicated that BA is a SIRT1 agonist in suppressing the HIF-1α signaling pathway to quell renal fibroblast activation and improve renal function in renal interstitial fibrosis.

title: Structure-constrained language-assisted diffusion model for unpaired low-dose computed tomography angiography reconstruction.
authors: Zhang G, Wang Z, Gao Z, Xu L, Zhou Z, Yu H, Zhang J, Liu X
journal: Neural networks : the official journal of the International Neural Network Society
abstract: The application of iodinated contrast media (ICM) improves the sensitivity and specificity of computed tomography (CT) for a wide range of clinical indications. However, high ICM doses can cause problems such as kidney damage and life-threatening allergic reactions. Deep learning methods can generate CT images of normal-dose ICM from low-dose ICM, reducing the required dose while maintaining diagnostic power. However, existing methods struggle to achieve accurate enhancement with incompletely paired images, mainly because of the limited ability of the model to recognize specific structures. To overcome this limitation, we propose a Structure-constrained Language-assisted Diffusion Model (SLDM), a unified medical generation model that integrates structural synergy and spatial intelligence. First, the structural prior information of the image is effectively extracted to constrain the model inference process, thus ensuring structural consistency in the enhancement process. Subsequently, a language-assisted strategy with spatial intelligence is introduced, which integrates the functions of visual perception and spatial reasoning, thus prompting the model to achieve accurate enhancement. Finally, the subtraction angiography enhancement module is applied, which serves to improve the contrast of the ICM region to suitable interval for observation. Qualitative analysis of visual comparison and quantitative results of several metrics demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in angiographic reconstruction for low-dose contrast medium CT angiography.

title: Nitroimidazole containing cyclicpeptide [68Ga]Ga-ZJUIQB-G002 as a new FAP-targeting radionuclide tracer.
authors: Guo Z, Zeng Y, Liu Z, Zhang G, Lin J, Shen Y, Ren E, Xu Q
abstract: Fibroblast activation protein (FAP) is one of the most extensively studied and promising targets for cancer diagnosis and therapy. Although small-molecule FAP-targeting radiopharmaceuticals are widely used, their clinical utility is often limited by rapid tumor washout and suboptimal therapeutic efficacy. To address these limitations, we designed a series of new FAP-targeting probes by incorporating a 2-nitroimidazole moiety into the FAP-2286 scaffold, a cyclic peptide known for prolonged tumor retention relative to conventional small-molecule FAP inhibitors. Among the resulting constructs, NOTA-ZJUIQB-G002 has potent hFAP-binding affinity (Kd = 0.032 nM), and [68Ga]Ga-NOTA-ZJUIQB-G002 exhibited markedly enhanced tumor uptake and improved tumor-to-background ratios (tumor/kidney > 3.0; tumor/intestine > 10.0) in PET studies using HEK293. hFAP xenograft models. The tracer also showed rapid clearance from most normal tissues while maintaining sustained tumor retention, resulting in favorable imaging contrast. In a more physiologically relevant U87 tumor-bearing mice without FAP gene transfection, [177Lu]Lu-DOTA-ZJUIQB-G002 exhibited improved tumor uptake but relatively higher renal uptake, highlighting the influence of tumor models on the in vivo pharmacokinetic behavior of FAP-targeting radioligands. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the potential of nitroimidazole-containing FAP-targeting radioligands for tumor imaging and future theranostic applications and support further investigation of this scaffold for FAP-targeted radiopharmaceutical development.

Redefining lifestyle interventions in the GLP-1-based therapies era.
authors: Namazi N, Larijani B
journal: Journal of diabetes and metabolic disorders
abstract: In response to the dramatic rise in obesity prevalence, associated morbidity, and healthcare costs worldwide, extensive research has focused on developing effective pharmacological treatments, including glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), for weight management and related complications. Despite the substantial weight loss and favorable effects on cardiometabolic risk factors associated with GLP-1 RAs, the importance of a healthy lifestyle, particularly adherence to healthy dietary patterns, remains undiminished. Rather, the role of nutrition needs to be redefined and emphasized as a central component of both weight loss and long-term weight maintenance. In this editorial, we aim to explore the evolving role of lifestyle modifications, with particular emphasis on nutritional considerations, in the era of GLP-1-based therapies.

title: Mortality patterns over two decades in U.S. adults with both diabetes and hypothyroidism: a retrospective analysis.
authors: Shahab SH, Naqvi SM, Hassan T, Umair E, Ahmed M, Hameem MZ, Khan AU, Ghani MZ
journal: Journal of diabetes and metabolic disorders
abstract: BACKGROUND: Hypothyroidism and diabetes mellitus frequently coexist and share autoimmune and metabolic pathways, yet population-level data on how their combined mortality burden has changed over time, and how it is distributed across demographic and geographic groups, remain limited. We examined national trends and disparities in mortality among United States (US) adults with both conditions. METHODS: In this retrospective, population-based analysis, death-certificate data for 1999-2023 were obtained from the Multiple Cause of Death database of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wide-ranging ONline Data for Epidemiologic Research (CDC WONDER). US resident decedents aged ≥ 25 years whose death certificates listed both hypothyroidism (International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision [ICD-10] code E03) and diabetes mellitus (E10-E14) as either the underlying or a contributing cause of death were included. Age-adjusted mortality rates (AAMRs) per 100,000 population, standardized to the 2000 US standard population, and crude mortality rates were calculated and stratified by sex, age, race and ethnicity, urban-rural status, census region, and state. Urban-rural and state-level analyses covered 1999-2020. Temporal trends were assessed with Joinpoint regression, yielding the annual percentage change (APC) for each segment and the average annual percentage change (AAPC) over the full period. A two-sided p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. RESULTS: A total of 119,113 deaths were identified over the 25-year period, with annual deaths rising from 2,934 in 1999 to 7,537 in 2023. The overall AAMR rose from 1.67 in 1999 to a peak of 3.10 in 2021 before declining slightly to 2.73 in 2023 (AAPC 1.86; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.88-2.85). Mortality was consistently higher in women than in men (AAMR 3.05 vs. 2.31 in 2023), although men showed a steeper long-term increase (AAPC 2.99; 95% CI 1.68-4.31 vs. 1.48; 95% CI 0.29-2.68). Older adults (≥ 65 years) carried an absolute burden roughly ten times that of middle-aged adults and far higher than that of young adults. The highest single-year rate among racial and ethnic groups occurred in the Hispanic or Latino population (4.28 in 2020), followed by White, Black or African American, and other groups; the long-term increase was significant among White individuals (AAPC 2.04; 95% CI 0.86-3.24) but not among Hispanic or Latino individuals (AAPC 1.95; 95% CI - 0.06 to 4.01). Rural (non-metropolitan) areas were disproportionately affected, peaking at 4.15 in 2020 versus 2.69 in urban areas (1999-2020 AAPC 3.26 vs. 2.14). The highest pooled state-level rates (1999-2020) were in West Virginia (4.16), North Dakota (3.65), and Ohio (3.57); by census region, the South showed the steepest long-term increase (AAPC 2.66; 95% CI 1.21-4.14) and the highest rate by 2023 (2.97), whereas the Midwest showed no significant long-term change. CONCLUSION: Mortality among US adults with coexisting hypothyroidism and diabetes increased significantly between 1999 and 2023, with a pronounced peak in 2021 and persistent disparities by sex, age, race and ethnicity, and geography. These findings support early thyroid screening in high-risk diabetic populations, equitable access to care, and region-specific prevention to reduce disparities and improve outcomes.

title: Synthetic CO2-fixation pathway empowers Yarrowia lipolytica for high-performance succinic acid biosynthesis.
authors: Sun T, Sun ML, Lin L, Wang K, Ledesma-Amaro R, Gao J, Ji XJ
abstract: Succinic acid, a bio-derived C4 platform chemical, has found widespread utility across multiple industrial domains, most notably in polymers, pharmaceuticals, and food processing, and its sustainable production via microbial fermentation has attracted increasing interest as an alternative to petrochemical synthesis. However, in aerobic Yarrowia lipolytica, succinic acid formation proceeding through the oxidative tricarboxylic acid (oTCA) pathway is constrained by substantial carbon loss. In this study, a heterologous phosphoribulokinase (Prk) -ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RuBisCo) CO2-fixation pathway was engineered in Y. lipolytica to enhance CO2 recycling and improve succinic acid biosynthesis from glycerol. The metabolic impacts of individual expression of Prk and RuBisCo genes were first assessed, followed by functional assembly of the complete Prk-RuBisCo pathway. Co-expression of Escherichia coli-derived GroEL/S chaperonins facilitated RuBisCo folding and further improved pathway efficiency. Moreover, increasing the copy numbers of RuBisCo and chaperone genes significantly enhanced CO2 recycling, which translated to an 8% improvement in succinic acid titer and a 32% gain in yield over the parental strain in shake flasks. Reduced glycerol consumption and decreased total by-product formation were also observed, indicating improved redox balancing through CO2 fixation. In a 5-L bioreactor operated under pH-unregulated conditions, strain ST-206 produced succinic acid at a final titer of 124.61 g/L, achieving a glycerol-to-product conversion of 0.46 g/g and a productivity of 0.88 g/(L·h). Collectively, this study reports the first successful establishment of a functional Prk-RuBisCo CO2-fixation pathway in Y. lipolytica, laying a metabolic and conceptual foundation for the future development of autotrophic Y. lipolytica strains.

title: Integrated distal enzyme engineering and intrinsically disordered peptide fusion enable efficient (-)-Germacrene D biosynthesis in Serratia marcescens.
authors: Xia B, Hu X, Wang L, Yang T, Zhou X, Wu S, Fan TP, Cai Y
abstract: (-)-Germacrene D is a bioactive sesquiterpene with demonstrated insect-repellent and behavioral regulatory activities. Here we report an integrated three-pronged strategy combining distal enzyme engineering, intrinsically disordered peptide (IDP) fusion, and pathway-level regulation to boost (-)-germacrene D production in the terpene-tolerant chassis Serratia marcescens HBQA7. A semi-rational distal mutagenesis pipeline-integrating spatial shell stratification, ConSurf conservation filtering, and Pythia folding ΔΔG screening-identified 58 candidate sites from 411 distal residues and yielded the double mutant XsGDSV52E/C183V with 2.5 g L-1 of (-)-germacrene D. N-terminal fusion of the NEXT IDP tag, selected from eight candidates, increased (-)-germacrene D production to 5.3 g L-1 without increasing the intrinsic catalytic efficiency of GDS. Promoter-based regulation of mvk using a stationary-phase promoter library further increased the titer to 6.3 g L-1. Fed-batch fermentation at the 5 L scale ultimately delivered 46.1 g L-1 of (-)-germacrene D with a glucose conversion yield of 16.2% (w/w)-the highest germacrene-type sesquiterpene titer reported to date.

title: Cortical spreading depression on Riemannian 2-manifolds: eikonal-curvature analysis and sulcal trapping.
authors: Enver A, Tepe N, Sara MY, Dilekoz E, Bolay H
abstract: Cortical spreading depression (CSD) is a slowly propagating wave of near-complete neuronal depolarization underlying migraine aura and implicated in stroke, traumatic brain injury, and subarachnoid hemorrhage. Existing reaction-diffusion models of CSD treat the cortex as a flat Euclidean domain, ignoring its highly folded, individually variable geometry. We develop a fully covariant FitzHugh-Nagumo (FHN) reaction-diffusion system on a smooth compact Riemannian 2-manifold [Formula: see text] representing the cortical sheet, in which the Euclidean Laplacian is replaced by the Laplace-Beltrami operator [Formula: see text]. Three mathematical results are established: (i) local and global well-posedness in [Formula: see text] together with positive invariance of the physiological region via parabolic semigroup theory; (ii) a curvature-corrected eikonal relation [Formula: see text], in which the wavefront speed is modulated by the geodesic curvature of the front; and (iii) a sulcal-trapping theorem giving an explicit criterion under which an excitable wave entering a sulcus (negative Gauss curvature region) remains confined to it. Numerically, we develop two complementary solvers: a discrete exterior calculus (DEC) scheme on triangulated surfaces using the cotangent Laplacian with implicit-explicit (IMEX) time-stepping, and a physics-informed neural network (PINN) surrogate that evaluates [Formula: see text] via the closest-point projection of the ambient Euclidean Laplacian. The PINN framework supports both forward simulation and the inverse identification of excitability fields from sparse observations, and a noise-ablation study quantifies its practical identifiability. The parameters of the slow subsystem and of the coupling functions are inherited from our published, cohort-calibrated thalamocortical model, which was calibrated against 67 paired-pulse somatosensory evoked potential (SEP) recordings from nine analysable animals of a cohort of 14 male Wistar rats (1, 233 sweeps) acquired in the Neuroscience Laboratory of Gazi University, with CSD induced by topical KCl application. We validate convergence on [Formula: see text] with the spectral ground-truth [Formula: see text], exhibit a propagating ring wave with a refractory tail, and verify the eikonal-curvature prediction across two orders of magnitude in geodesic curvature, including the leading correction due to the recovery variable; a mesh-convergence study yields explicit resolution requirements for evaluating the trapping criterion on MRI-derived cortical surfaces.

title: Feedback as automatic dose selection in a basal ganglia-thalamocortical model of adaptive deep brain stimulation.
authors: Nawaz A, Shareef Z, Ahmed I, Gdeisat M, Hai N, Fayyaz Z, Numan A, Al Bataineh A
abstract: We separate the effects of feedback and of stimulation dose in adaptive deep brain stimulation (DBS), using a seven-population firing-rate model of the basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop. A closed-loop advantage may reflect dose rather than feedback. The model has dopamine-dependent gains, delays, a prescribed 20-Hz beta input, and a suppressive input to the subthalamic nucleus set by a saturated proportional-integral (PI) controller on thalamic output. Dose is the command amplitude, and four constant commands are matched to the closed loop on late command, cumulative command, stimulation use, and full-horizon error. An exact window identity for integral action and a convexity condition, under which a constant command is quasi-statically at least as efficient as any time-varying command within the convex range at a fixed state, define when an advantage reflects dose. At five dopamine levels and three horizons, a constant command with equal stimulation use had lower full-horizon error than the closed loop in all 15 comparisons, and the closed loop settled within 0.004 of the constant command required. In a 200-subject cohort varying 20 parameters, including time constants and delays, the individually optimized constant command had lower error than feedback at a fixed state in all 200 subjects. After dopamine fell and recovered, the closed loop had lower error than the best constant after the change in 185, and over whole runs including its start-up, than the best constant for the schedule in 96. In this model, feedback acts as automatic dose selection whose benefit appears when the disease state changes.

title: Dynamical mechanisms of pathological phase-amplitude coupling in a network comprising subthalamic and two types of globus pallidus neurons.
authors: Yang J, Shi X, Wang L
abstract: Pathologically enhanced β oscillations and their cross-frequency coupling with high-frequency oscillations is a hallmark of Parkinson's disease, yet its dynamical origins remain elusive, partly due to oversimplified modeling of the GPe as a homogeneous nucleus. In this study, we developed a biophysical STN-heterogeneous GPe network model incorporating prototypic (TI) and arkypallidal (TA) neurons to investigate the phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) generation and the differential roles of intra-loop pathways. Our results show that the STN-TI-STN sub-loop serves as the core dynamical substrate for generating and sustaining pathological PAC. TA neurons do not drive PAC but potentiate it via lateral inhibition onto TI, with their drive originating from STN input. Selective TI excitation abolishes PAC, whereas TA stimulation is ineffective. The consistent evolution of synchronization index, β power, and modulation index supports PAC as a reliable feedback biomarker. This work points to a new network mechanism of PAC generation within the STN-heterogeneous GPe network, identifies the TI subpopulation as a promising target for precision optogenetic intervention, and provides theoretical foundations for developing adaptive DBS strategies guided by PAC-based feedback signals.

title: A benchmarking framework for organoid computing.
authors: Xing Y, Gao Y, Hong Z, Tian C, Cai H, Chu H, Yang Y, Liang PY
abstract: Organoid computing leverages functional neural networks of lab-grown neural organoids to recapitulate key aspects of human brain information processing, holding promising potential in brain-inspired computing, brain-computer interfaces, neuroscience, and medicine. However, its broad application remains constrained due to technical limitations including biological variability, interface instability, stochastic performance, and limited reproducibility. Here, we present a benchmarking framework that systematically quantifies the key performance determinants of organoid computing. We operationally define 'benchmark-ready' organoid substrates using optional criteria encompassing viability, cellular identity, structural integrity, functional maturation, and baseline networks, supported by multimodal phenotyping. We further establish qualification metrics for organoid-machine interface and intrinsic neural and network function, including physical coupling, spatial coverage, temporal stability, spontaneous activity, and network-level organization. Finally, we introduce a hierarchical evaluation framework for stimulation-evoked computation combined with information encoding criteria, standardized scoring, and statistical reporting. We believe that the benchmarking framework may provide an adaptable foundation for standardized, reproducible and comparable evaluation of organoid computing technologies, thereby facilitating the broad adoption and application of organoid intelligence.

title: Comparative effects of Etanercept and Tocilizumab on skeletal muscle fibers in aged zebrafish.
authors: Abbaspour F, Shokrpoor S, Delgarm A, Razi F, Heshmat R, Mohammadi H, Shafiee G
journal: Journal of diabetes and metabolic disorders
abstract: BACKGROUND: Sarcopenia, the age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass and function, is increasingly recognized as a major contributor to disability and mortality. Chronic low-grade inflammation, including signaling involving tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6), has been linked to age-related muscle loss. We evaluated whether Etanercept, a TNF-α inhibitor, and Tocilizumab, an IL-6 receptor antagonist, affected skeletal muscle fiber number and the qualitative infiltration of inflammatory cells in aged zebrafish. METHODS: One hundred wild-type AB zebrafish aged 35-40 months were allocated to five groups (n = 20/group): untreated control, Etanercept 0.8 mg/kg/week, Etanercept 1.6 mg/kg/week, Tocilizumab 4 mg/kg/2 weeks, and Tocilizumab 8 mg/kg/2 weeks. Treatment continued for 3 months. Dorsal skeletal muscle was assessed histologically for cross-sectional area (CSA), number of fibers, and qualitative inflammatory-cell infiltration. RESULTS: Eighty-two of 100 fish survived to study completion. Mean measured dorsal muscle CSA was higher in the Etanercept 0.8 mg/kg group (6.56 ± 0.28 mm²) and the Tocilizumab 8 mg/kg group (5.82 ± 0.40 mm²) than in controls (5.10 ± 0.19 mm², P < 0.001). Etanercept 0.8 mg/kg-treated fish had fewer fibers in the 10,000 μm² sampling area than controls (approximately 26 vs. 57, P < 0.001). Qualitative histology showed minimal or absent inflammatory-cell infiltration in the Etanercept 0.8 mg/kg group. Etanercept 1.6 mg/kg-treated fish had greater endpoint body weight than controls. CONCLUSION: In aged zebrafish, selected Etanercept and Tocilizumab regimens were associated with differences in measured skeletal muscle fiber characteristics and body weight. Low-dose Etanercept was associated with a higher CSA of the dorsal muscle and a lower number of fibers within the standardized sampling area. These findings represent exploratory histological associations and do not establish preservation of total muscle mass, muscle function, or a specific molecular mechanism. The absence of young controls, functional testing, quantitative inflammatory assessment, and molecular validation limits mechanistic and translational interpretation.

title: Circulating LRG1 in heart failure: association with type 2 diabetes and antidiabetic therapy class.
authors: Alrosan K, Odeh M, Alqudah A, Abudalo R, Qnais E
journal: Journal of diabetes and metabolic disorders
abstract: BACKGROUND: Heart failure (HF) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) frequently coexist and share remodelling and inflammatory mechanisms. Although leucine-rich α-2 glycoprotein 1 (LRG1) has been identified as a biomarker associated with vascular remodelling, fibrosis, and inflammation, its role in HF patients with type 2 diabetes and its connection to antidiabetic treatments remains unclear. METHODS: 115 patients with HF were divided into three groups for this cross-sectional study: HF who had no previously documented diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and were not receiving antidiabetic medication at enrolment (n = 42), HF with T2DM treated with DPP-4 inhibitors (n = 35), and HF with T2DM treated with SGLT-2 inhibitors (n = 38). The groups' clinical characteristics, metabolic parameters, and circulating LRG1 levels were compared. RESULTS: LRG1 levels differed significantly across the groups (p = 0.002), with the lowest levels observed in the SGLT-2 inhibitor group. A post hoc analysis revealed a significant difference between the SGLT-2 inhibitor group and group of no previously documented diagnosis of diabetes mellitus (p = 0.001). No significant correlations were observed between LRG1 and clinical or metabolic variables. CONCLUSION: Circulating LRG1 levels in HF patients differed between study groups, with the lowest levels observed in the SGLT-2 inhibitor group. These findings suggest an association between treatment group and LRG1 levels, but the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference regarding the effects of antidiabetic medications on inflammatory and remodelling pathways.

title: Engineered microorganisms drive local metabolic reprogramming to Re-educate systemic immunity.
authors: Ma Y, Yang Y, Yu Z, Jin M, Jin Y, Wang J, Wang H, Zhao Q
abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) features chronic synovial inflammation and systemic immune disorders. Current treatments mainly rely on systemic immunosuppression, raising risks of infection and long-term immune injury. Local therapies reduce such risks but struggle to regulate systemic immunity. Emerging studies show the synovial immunometabolic microenvironment links local inflammation to systemic responses. Here, we developed a strategy based on chemically attenuated photosynthetic bacteria that couples lactate metabolism with photo-driven hydrogen production to achieve local metabolic reprogramming and systemic immune re-education. We screened a photosynthetic bacterial strain with high lactate metabolic capacity, which also exhibited enhanced hydrogen production. To ensure safety, bacteria were PEGylated to mask immunogenic moieties while preserving metabolic activity. Intra-articular injection disrupted pathological crosstalk and restored the Treg/Th17 balance locally. Circulating IL-6 levels decreased, restoring the systemic regulatory role of Tregs, thereby alleviating distant joint inflammation. These results demonstrate that local synovial metabolic reprogramming by engineered bacteria can induce systemic immune re-education, offering a conceptually new therapeutic strategy for treating autoimmune arthritis.

title: Long-term Endoscopic Evolution of a Pyloric Gland Adenoma Arising in Nonatrophic Gastric Mucosa and Initially Resembling a Fundic Gland Polyp.
authors: Kobayashi R, Nakanishi H, Takaura K, Tanaka S, Maeyashiki C, Tamaki N, Yasui Y, Sakurai U
abstract: Pyloric gland adenoma (PGA) is a rare gastric epithelial neoplasm often associated with autoimmune or metaplastic atrophic gastritis. An 80-year-old man underwent serial upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. A small gastric fundus lesion initially resembling a fundic gland polyp (FGP) was followed without biopsy. Over 11 years, it enlarged to 22 mm and became increasingly whitish, against a background described endoscopically as nonatrophic. Biopsy suggested PGA, and the lesion was resected en bloc by endoscopic submucosal dissection. Closely packed pyloric-type glands showed elongation, tortuosity, branching, and cystic dilatation, with diffuse MUC6 expression and MUC5AC expression restricted to the surface epithelium. The lesion was diagnosed as PGA with low-grade dysplasia. The adjacent oxyntic mucosa showed no atrophy, lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, or nodular enterochromaffin-like cell hyperplasia. Without an initial biopsy, whether the lesion was already PGA or developed within a pre-existing FGP remains unknown. An enlarging or increasingly whitish FGP-like lesion warrants histologic assessment, even in nonatrophic gastric mucosa.
